name: ngtcp2
workload: quicperf: an apples-to-apples C++ benchmark harness running the same shared TLS material, saturation policy, and socket backend (syscall/io_uring) against native adapters for ngtcp2, LSQUIC, TQUIC, quiche, picoquic, XQUIC and several Rust/Zig stacks, over loopback UDP with CUBIC congestion control. Scenarios include bulk download/upload, bidirectional transfer, multistream transfer, loss recovery, and flow-control-limited transfer.
claimed_speedup: ~1.6-2.1x quiche on bulk-transfer scenarios (p50, syscall backend, derived from page data): download 18.227 vs 11.258 Gbps, upload 31.047 vs 14.794 Gbps, bidirectional 20.503 vs 12.662 Gbps, multistream upload 24.816 vs 15.291 Gbps, loss-recovery 17.379 vs 11.689 Gbps, flow-control 15.600 vs 10.309 Gbps
compiler_and_flags: quicperf C++ harness: Release build, -O3, native CPU flags, LTO by default (per README); quiche's Rust packet engine built via quicperf depofile with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native -C opt-level=3", CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=fat, CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_CODEGEN_UNITS=1
tradeoffs: C library requiring an external TLS backend (OpenSSL/BoringSSL/GnuTLS/wolfSSL/picotls) and manual event-loop integration, unlike quiche's more batteries-included Rust API. In the same quicperf harness ngtcp2 is markedly slower than quiche and most peers on connection-establishment rate (113 vs 277 conn/s, syscall) and on plain request/response rate (51,386 vs 64,574 rps), so its measured advantage is specific to sustained bulk-transfer throughput, not connection setup or small-request rate.
caveats: quicperf's committed run-environment file (docs/results/fixed-full-matrix-max16-20260601T175816Z/fixed-environment.txt) records only an anonymized machine_hash, with no CPU model, so hardware is not stated -- this caps the entry at Tier B despite public benchmark code and documented build flags. Benchmark is loopback-only (not a physical/WAN link). Several ngtcp2 rows in this table are flagged 'inconclusive' (tripped a CI/spread/drift gate) rather than 'publishable', though ngtcp2's lead over quiche held in both the inconclusive and publishable rows across syscall and io_uring backends.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "ngtcp2" "benchmark" -> victorstewart/quicperf; numbers read directly from docs/latest-results.md and docs/methodology.md

name: TQUIC
workload: quicperf: same shared C++ harness as the ngtcp2 entry above, measuring fresh-stream HTTP-style request/response rate, stream churn (open/send/receive/finish), tiny-message rate, and 0-RTT request/response under a 16-client-thread saturation scout, over loopback UDP.
claimed_speedup: ~2.1-2.4x quiche on request/message-rate scenarios (p50, syscall backend, derived from page data): request/response 155,043 vs 64,574 rps, stream churn 178,272 vs 74,756 streams/s, small-payload messages 176,604 vs 73,852 msgs/s, 0-RTT request/response 154,448 vs 65,327 rps
compiler_and_flags: TQUIC built via quicperf depofile with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native -C opt-level=3", CARGO_BUILD env BORINGSSL_LIB_DIR set, CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=fat, CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_CODEGEN_UNITS=1; C++ harness built -O3/native CPU flags/LTO by default
tradeoffs: Implemented in Rust (exposes C/C++ FFI, not a native C++ library). In the same harness TQUIC loses to quiche on raw bulk download throughput (8.6-8.9 vs 9.8-11.3 Gbps) and on resumed-connection rate (216 vs 306 conn/s, syscall), so its measured edge is specific to request/response and stream-churn rate, not bulk transfer.
caveats: Same anonymized-hardware limitation as the ngtcp2 entry above (no CPU model recorded in quicperf's committed environment file) caps this at Tier B. TQUIC also publishes its own first-party benchmark (https://tquic.net/docs/further_readings/benchmark) claiming to be 'four to five times faster' than Google's QUICHE-G and 'up to 20%' faster than LSQUIC on an AMD EPYC 7K62 testbed, but that page gives only chart images (no raw numbers or benchmark source) and compares against QUICHE-G/nginx-quic/LSQUIC rather than Cloudflare's quiche directly -- first-party only, so on its own it would rate Tier C; it is not used as the primary evidence here.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "ngtcp2" "benchmark" -> victorstewart/quicperf docs/latest-results.md; corroborated by TQUIC's own README benchmark link

name: LSQUIC
workload: "QUIC on the Highway" (Koenig, Zirngibl et al., ACM IMC 2023): an adaptation of the QUIC Interop Runner run on dedicated (non-virtualized) 10G-linked physical hosts, measuring HTTP/3 goodput for six QUIC implementations (aioquic, quic-go, mvfst, picoquic, quiche, LSQUIC) across buffer-size configurations.
claimed_speedup: ~1.28x quiche with buffer tuning (derived from page data): verbatim, "LSQUIC reaches a goodput of 3250 Mbit/s, an 8.7% increase compared to the baseline" (largest tested buffer) vs quiche buffer tuning that "increase[s] the goodput but only by 3% to 2530 Mbit/s"; the paper separately states goodput across all six implementations and buffer settings ranges "52 Mbit/s to 3004 Mbit/s", and names LSQUIC and quiche as "the two best-performing implementations" of the six tested
hardware: AMD EPYC 7543 (32-core), 512GB RAM, Broadcom BCM57416 NICs as primary configuration; additional runs on AMD EPYC 7551P and several Intel Xeon models
tradeoffs: The margin over quiche here is narrow (~1.28x) and buffer-tuning-dependent, not a decisive win; the paper frames LSQUIC and quiche as roughly co-best of the six implementations it tested, not LSQUIC as a clear outright leader.
caveats: LSQUIC is already catalogued on KNOWN_LIST; included here only as new Tier B evidence of it beating the in-scope baseline quiche, per the orchestrator's is_evidence_for_known exception (GitHub hosts the paper's companion benchmark/analysis code at https://github.com/tumi8/quic-10g-paper, which is public but has no declared license and was not independently checked for exact compiler/flag settings used per-implementation, capping this at Tier B rather than A despite public code and stated CPU hardware).
